title: Delegates inside out
sub: The delegate class, chains, exceptions and explicit add/remove
cards/0/title: One delegate line is a whole class
cards/0/body:
The declaration delegate int Op(int a, int b); is not a "function type" but a class. The compiler generates a sealed class Op deriving from System.MulticastDelegate, with four methods:

  • a constructor (object, IntPtr) — an object and a method address;
  • Invoke(int a, int b) — with the same signature as the delegate;
  • BeginInvoke and EndInvoke — old-style asynchronous invocation.

These methods have no bodies: they are marked runtime managed, and the CLR supplies their code. Func and Action are the same kind of class, just already declared in the library.
cards/0/deep:
The compiler turns op(2, 3) into callvirt Op::Invoke. The JIT does not call Invoke like an ordinary method: it reads the object and the code address from the delegate and makes an indirect call — close to a virtual call in cost. The JIT usually cannot inline a delegate's target; with dynamic PGO (.NET 8+) it sometimes inserts a "is it that same method" check and a direct call — guarded devirtualization for delegates.

On .NET Framework, BeginInvoke ran the delegate on the thread pool through the remoting infrastructure. On .NET Core and later the method is still in the metadata but throws PlatformNotSupportedException. The replacement is Task.Run(() => op(2, 3)).
cards/1/q: What does the compiler turn op(2, 3) into, where op is a variable of type Op?
cards/1/options/2: A direct call to the target method
cards/1/explain: Invoking a delegate is always a call to its Invoke method. The compiler does not know what will be inside the delegate: that is decided at run time.
cards/1/wrong/1: DynamicInvoke is a slow reflection-based call with an argument array. The compiler never uses it on its own.
cards/1/wrong/2: Which method the delegate holds is known only at run time.
cards/2/title: Inside: an object and a code address
cards/2/body:
A delegate instance is a heap object. It inherits two key fields from System.Delegate:

  • _target — the object to call an instance method on;
  • _methodPtr — the address of the method's machine code.

From outside you see them as the Target and Method properties. For a static method Target returns null. Creating a delegate in IL is ldftn (take the method address) plus newobj on the constructor: one allocation.
cards/2/deep:
A delegate to a static method is trickier inside: the real address sits in _methodPtrAux, while _methodPtr holds a small shuffle thunk that shifts the arguments, since there is no receiver object. The Target property still returns null. Because of the thunk, a delegate to a static method is slightly more expensive to call than one to an instance method.

That is why the C# compiler turns capture-free lambdas into instance methods of a hidden singleton class <>c and caches the delegate itself in a static field: creating it again does not allocate. Since C# 11 a static method group conversion is cached the same way (Func<int, int> f = Math.Abs;).
cards/3/options/0: False: Target is an instance of the hidden <>c class
cards/3/options/1: True: a capture-free lambda compiles to a static method
cards/3/options/2: False: Target is the delegate twice itself
cards/3/options/3: Does not compile: a lambda has no Target
cards/3/explain: The C# compiler places capture-free lambdas in instance methods of the <>c singleton: a delegate to an instance method needs no argument-shuffling thunk. Target is that singleton.
cards/3/wrong/1: It sounds logical, but the compiler avoids it on purpose: a delegate to a static method goes through a thunk and is slightly slower.
cards/4/title: A chain is a new object
cards/4/body:
a += b means a = (Action)Delegate.Combine(a, b). Combine changes neither a nor b: delegates are immutable. It creates a new delegate that holds an array inside — the invocation list of all methods in order.

-= is Delegate.Remove: also a new object, without the last occurrence of the method. Remove the last method and you get null.

Two consequences. Every += is an allocation, and a chain also has an array. And a copy of the delegate in another variable does not see new subscriptions: it points to the old object.
cards/4/deep:
In MulticastDelegate the chain lives in the _invocationList field (an object[] of delegates) and _invocationCount. Combine with null returns the other argument without allocating. When appending, the runtime can reuse an array with spare room if the next slot in it is still free — so a series of += does not copy the whole list every time.

Immutability makes invocation thread-safe: handler?.Invoke() works on one snapshot of the chain even if another thread is unsubscribing right now. That is why the old advice "copy the event to a local before the null check" boils down to ?. today.
cards/5/explain: copy = log copies a reference to a single-method delegate. Each += creates a new chain and stores it only in its own variable: log is 1 and 2, copy is 1 and 3.
cards/5/wrong/1: That would be true if += appended the method to a shared object. But delegates are immutable.
cards/6/title: Exceptions and results in a chain
cards/6/body:
Invoke on a chain is a loop over the invocation list. Hence behavior that is easy to forget:

  • An exception in the second method breaks the loop. The third and later ones are not called, and the exception flies to whoever invoked the delegate.
  • The return value comes from the last method; the other results are discarded. Each next method sees ref and out parameters already changed by the previous one.

If you need to call everyone independently or collect all results, walk GetInvocationList() yourself.
cards/7/q: On which line does Console.WriteLine never run?
cards/7/explain: The chain calls the methods in turn: "step 1", then the exception. The third method is never called — the exception has left Invoke. catch prints "error", then "done".
cards/8/q: Collect the results of all checks, not just the last one
cards/8/explain: GetInvocationList returns an array of delegates, one method each. Their Invoke returns its own bool. DynamicInvoke would return object — it does not go into a List<bool> without a cast, and a reflection call is slow anyway.
cards/9/title: An event with explicit add and remove
cards/9/body:
An ordinary event public event EventHandler? Changed; is expanded by the compiler into a private delegate field and two accessor methods: add_Changed and remove_Changed. Those are what += and -= call from outside.

You can write the accessors yourself — like get and set on a property. Then the compiler creates no field, and you decide where subscribers live: in one dictionary for all events, in another object, in weak references.
cards/9/deep:
Since C# 4 the generated add of an ordinary event takes no lock: in a loop it reads the field, calls Delegate.Combine and tries to store the result with Interlocked.CompareExchange until nobody interferes. Subscribing from different threads is safe. In your own accessors thread safety is on you — the dictionary in the example does not provide it.

Why bother: a class with a hundred events that usually nobody subscribes to would spend a field per event in every object. Windows Forms controls therefore keep subscribers in a single EventHandlerList. In metadata an event is an .event record linking the name to the add_ and remove_ methods.
cards/10/q: Which line inside the Panel class does not compile?
cards/10/explain: An event with explicit accessors has no field behind the name Resized. Even inside the class it can only appear on the left of += and -= (error CS0079). You invoke the delegate you store yourself — _resized.
cards/11/pairs/0/1: The object to call the method on
cards/11/pairs/2/1: A new delegate with an invocation list
cards/11/pairs/3/1: The chain's delegates one by one
cards/12/options/0: += on a delegate creates a new object; the old one does not change
cards/12/options/1: If the second method in a chain throws, the third still runs
cards/12/options/2: A delegate class derives from MulticastDelegate and is sealed
cards/12/options/3: In .NET 8 BeginInvoke runs the delegate on the thread pool
cards/12/options/4: An event with explicit add and remove cannot be invoked by name
cards/12/explain: An exception breaks the chain: the remaining methods are not called. On .NET Core and later BeginInvoke throws PlatformNotSupportedException — use Task.Run instead.
